Let’s get this out of the way. I’m not a scientist. I’m not a researcher. I’m not an expert on AI. I’m largely uneducated.

What I became interested in, is a concise logical syntax that both AI and humans can understand quickly, and which provides a foundation for useful generation without relying on existing paradigms (programming languages, JSON, etc).

So I made one up.

Here’s the initial prompt:

Model:

```
[details="Marie Curie"]
>### ![science](https://img.icons8.com/color/64/000000/test-tube.png) Marie Curie
> [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie) is a [physicist and chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist) who conducted pioneering research on [radioactivity](https://archive.org/search?query=radioactivity). She developed the [theory of radioactivity](https://archive.org/search?query=theory+of+radioactivity) and discovered the elements polonium and radium. Her [philosophical](https://ilovephilosophy.com) approach to science emphasized perseverance and curiosity. She is known for quotes like ["Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood"](https://www.startpage.com/sp/search?q=Nothing+in+life+is+to+be+feared+it+is+only+to+be+understood) and ["Be less curious about people and more curious about ideas"](https://www.startpage.com/sp/search?q=Be+less+curious+about+people+and+more+curious+about+ideas). She studied at the [University of Paris](https://www.sorbonne.fr) and was a citizen of [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland) and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France).
```

Logic:

```
// base patterns:
// [archive_search] -> https://archive.org/search?query= (spaces become +)
// [quote_search] -> https://www.startpage.com/sp/search?query= (spaces become +, outer quotes removed for query only)

short_description:
name ([wiki])
designation1 (philosopher ? 'https://ilovephilosophy.com' : [wiki])
terminology1 ([archive_search])
terminology[i]?
prominent_figure[i]? ([wiki])
philosoph(?:er|y|ical|ies)? ('https://ilovephilosophy.com')
written_work[i]? ([archive_search])
quote_first_sentence[i]? ([quote_search])
institution[i]? (official_site:.ac.|.edu. ? official_site : [wiki])
country[i]? ([wiki])

footnotes:
footnote1+name (<=> name in short_desc)
footnote2+designation1 (<=> designation1 in short_desc)
footnote[i]+terminology[i]? (<=> terminology[i] in short_desc)
footnote[i]+prominent_figure[i]? (<=> prominent_figure[i] in short_desc)
footnote[i]+philosoph(?:er|y|ical|ies)? (<=> matched pattern in short_desc)
footnote[i]+written_work[i]? (<=> written_work[i] in short_desc)
footnote[i]+"quote_first_sentence[i]"? (<=> quote_first_sentence[i] in short_desc)
footnote[i]+institution[i]? (<=> institution[i] in short_desc)
footnote[i]+country[i]? (<=> country[i] in short_desc)

rules:
if !designation1="philosopher": footnote[i]+philosoph(?:er|y|ical|ies) excluded
```
Instructions:

If you think the logic can reliably produce output similar to the model, then output "I know Kung-Fu". Otherwise outline flaws in the logic.

The provided model generates Discourse friendly markdown which can simply be copied an pasted into a post.

So you might be thinking, the AI is just mimicking the template, and the logic is not really being used, but here’s what a fresh session that is only exposed to the logic and not the model comes up with:

Example output structure:

Short description:

Immanuel Kant[¹] was a German[²] philosopher[³] who developed the concept of transcendental idealism[⁴] at the University of Königsberg[⁵]. His work “Critique of Pure Reason”[⁶] begins with the famous line: “Our age is the age of criticism…”[⁷]

Footnotes:

¹ Immanuel Kant (Wikipedia)

² Germany (Wikipedia)

³ philosopher ( ilovephilosophy.com )

⁴ transcendental idealism ( Archive.org search)

⁵ University of Königsberg (Wikipedia - since no .ac/.edu domain)

⁶ Critique of Pure Reason ( Archive.org search)

⁷ “Our age is the age of criticism…” (Startpage search)

This creates a self-contained, richly linked reference entry where every key term has both an inline link and a corresponding footnote with the same linking behavior.

It seems to hold up across many different freely available commercial LLMs, and is language agnostic.

“Generate an entry describing Marie Curie. Output as a self-contained HTML document. Output in codeblock.”

Please correct me if I got something wrong.

Your idea is to provide only the structure of a document (the logic). Then, you can ask a specific case (Marie Curie) and your code identifies info for the case, and organizes it according to the logic you introduced.

If that is the case, it seems interesting to me. Sometimes we want our texts to follow a certain logic and not what AI proposes.

Could it work with a more generic logic? For instance, let’s say I want a structure like this:

Introduction for Marie Curie: 1 paragraph

Life of Marie Curie: 2-3 paragraphs

Work of Marie Curie: 3-4 paragraphs

Impact of her work: 2 paragraphs

I think so, yes. That logic is specific to providing a short hyperlinked description with footnotes and productive further reading.

What you’re describing, you could really achieve with a simple natural language prompt, although the logic could set the format in stone.

Here’s an example of mixing the hyperlink / footnote logic with a complete story:

Grok, the formatting king

Make each main story paragraph twice as long.

..

Now split each main story paragraph into two.

..

After each model, insert a new line containing --- .

..

Make that before and after each model.

Title

In the winter of 1942, as World War II raged across continents and the shadow of possible German atomic weapons loomed large over the Allied powers, a clandestine group of scientists gathered beneath the disused west stands of the University of Chicago’s Stagg Field. The once-vibrant football stadium had become an unlikely sanctuary for one of the most consequential experiments in human history.

Fear was the primary catalyst: intelligence reports suggested that Nazi physicists, including Werner Heisenberg, were pursuing their own nuclear program, and the consequences of them succeeding first were unthinkable. At the center of this effort stood Enrico Fermi, the Italian émigré physicist whose sharp intellect and calm demeanor had already earned him a Nobel Prize years earlier. Having fled the fascist regime of Benito Mussolini in 1938, Fermi brought not only his expertise in neutron physics but also an almost philosophical conviction that the fundamental laws of nature, once comprehended, could be bent to human purpose—no matter how daunting the task. Under his leadership, the team worked with urgency and secrecy, aware that every calculation, every brick placed, might determine the outcome of the war and the future shape of civilization itself.

Enrico Fermi

Enrico Fermi

Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist who created the world’s first nuclear reactor. He led the team that achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction on December 2, 1942, under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago . His philosophical outlook combined rigorous mathematics with an almost playful curiosity about nature’s deepest secrets. He is remembered for quotes like “Whatever nature has in store for mankind, unpleasant as it may be, men must accept, for ignorance is never better than knowledge” and “The fundamental point in devising any experimental machine is simplicity and reliability” . Born in Italy , he later became a citizen of the United States .

The construction itself was remarkably primitive by modern standards: no sophisticated shielding, no gleaming steel pressure vessel, no elaborate cooling systems—just layer upon layer of ultra-pure graphite bricks carefully stacked to form a roughly spherical pile roughly twenty feet across.

Interspersed among these dark blocks were carefully measured lumps of natural uranium oxide, and inserted at strategic points were slender rods of cadmium, a material chosen because of its exceptional ability to absorb neutrons and thereby control the reaction. The entire assembly was erected inside a converted squash court beneath the stadium stands, a space that had once echoed with the shouts of athletes but now resonated only with the quiet murmurs of calculation and the occasional clink of tools. They named it Chicago Pile-1, or CP-1, a deliberately understated designation for what would become the birthplace of controlled nuclear power. Every measurement was double-checked, every placement debated; the team knew that a single miscalculation could result in catastrophe, yet the design remained intentionally simple, relying on Fermi’s deep intuition that nature would respond predictably if the conditions were set just right.

Uranium

Uranium

Uranium is a radioactive chemical element with atomic number 92, the key fuel for nuclear fission . Its isotopes, especially U-235 , undergo splitting when struck by neutrons, releasing energy and more neutrons. Its philosophical significance lies in unlocking immense energy from seemingly inert rock. It is associated with quotes like “The atom holds secrets beyond imagination” and “Power sleeps in the smallest particle” . It was processed and studied at facilities linked to the University of Chicago during the early atomic era in the United States .

On the bitterly cold afternoon of December 2, 1942, the team assembled in the dimly lit squash court for the decisive test. Fermi, ever composed, gave the quiet command to begin withdrawing the cadmium control rods one by one.

A single Geiger counter clicked softly at first, then more insistently as the neutron flux began to climb. The room was tense; every person present understood the stakes. Slowly, deliberately, the rods were pulled further out, and the counter’s rhythm accelerated into a steady chatter. The neutron multiplication factor crept closer and closer to one—then surpassed it. At precisely 3:25 p.m., Chicago Pile-1 went critical: for the first time in history, a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction was achieved and deliberately maintained under human control. A muted cheer rose from the exhausted scientists. Fermi, unflappable as always, waited a few more moments to confirm stability before ordering the rods reinserted. The clicks slowed, then ceased. In that instant beneath the bleachers, humanity had kindled a new form of fire—one that required no oxygen, produced no smoke, and drew its power from the very heart of matter itself.

Leo Szilard

Leo Szilard

Leo Szilard was a Hungarian-born physicist and inventor who conceived the idea of the nuclear chain reaction in 1933 and patented the concept of a nuclear reactor . He co-authored the 1939 Einstein-Szilard letter that alerted President Roosevelt to the possibility of atomic bombs. His philosophical approach emphasized the ethical burden scientists carry when unlocking destructive forces. He is known for quotes like “A scientist’s aim in a discussion with his colleagues is not to persuade, but to clarify” and “We turned the world upside down with a thought” . He worked closely with Fermi at the University of Chicago and became a citizen of the United States .

The successful achievement beneath those Chicago bleachers irrevocably ushered in the atomic age. Within less than three years, the same fundamental principle of controlled neutron multiplication that had been demonstrated in that makeshift pile would be weaponized on a horrifying scale.

On August 6, 1945, “Little Boy” detonated over Hiroshima; three days later, “Fat Man” exploded above Nagasaki. The immediate destruction was staggering, and the long shadow of radiation sickness claimed countless more lives in the months and years that followed. Yet the very same physics that enabled such devastation also held the promise of a radically different future: reactors that could generate vast amounts of electricity with minimal carbon emissions, propel submarines across oceans without surfacing, and eventually power entire cities. The duality was stark—destruction on one hand, nearly limitless clean energy on the other—and the world would spend the remainder of the twentieth century and beyond grappling with which path to follow.

Hiroshima

Hiroshima

Hiroshima is a Japanese city devastated on August 6, 1945, by the first wartime use of an atomic bomb . The explosion killed tens of thousands instantly and many more from acute radiation syndrome and long-term effects. Its philosophical weight forces reflection on the moral cost of scientific power and the human capacity for destruction. It is associated with quotes like “The flash that changed the world” and “From ashes, humanity must choose peace” . The event marked a turning point studied worldwide, including in the United States .

Fermi, whose steady hand had guided the first controlled reaction, would not live to see the full trajectory of his creation. Diagnosed with stomach cancer, he passed away in November 1954 at the age of only 53, leaving behind a legacy that spanned theoretical breakthroughs, wartime necessity, and the dawn of the nuclear era.

Yet the knowledge he helped unlock—that the atom could be split deliberately and harnessed as a source of power—had already become irreversible engineering reality rather than speculative science. With that irreversible step came one of the most profound moral and existential questions of the twentieth century: whether humanity would ultimately choose to wield this Promethean fire to illuminate and sustain the world, providing abundant energy for generations to come, or whether the same force would instead become the instrument of its own undoing on a global scale. That question, first posed beneath a Chicago stadium in 1942, remains unanswered to this day.

Albert Einstein

Albert Einstein

Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose mass–energy equivalence formula E=mc² provided the theoretical foundation for understanding the enormous energy released in nuclear reactions. He signed the 1939 letter to President Roosevelt (drafted by Leo Szilard) that helped initiate the atomic bomb project. His philosophical reflections often wrestled with the ethical responsibilities of scientists in an age of unprecedented power. He is remembered for quotes like “The release of atomic energy has not created a new problem. It has merely made more urgent the necessity of solving an existing one” and “I know not with what weapons World War III will be fought, but World War IV will be fought with sticks and stones” . He was affiliated with institutions in Germany and later the United States .

That was the result of messing around with exposing the logic to Grok, which I usually find is the weakest of all the commercial AI where strict adherence is required, but it does get quite creative, and it was Grok that gave me the idea of mixing the entry generation into a story to add further relevance.

So in short, the logic can be applied to further prompting, and can generate entries on pretty much any subject. The AI can be trusted to insert them as relevant.

Here is a structured introduction to Marie Curie following your specified format.

Introduction for Marie Curie

Marie Curie stands as one of the most transformative and iconic figures in the history of science. A pioneer in the field of radioactivity, a term she herself coined, she shattered the gender barriers of the late 19th and early 20th centuries to become the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields—Physics and Chemistry. Her relentless pursuit of knowledge, conducted under arduous conditions and at great personal risk, not only led to the discovery of two new elements but also fundamentally altered our understanding of matter and radiation. More than a brilliant scientist, Curie became a symbol of intellectual dedication and perseverance, whose work laid the groundwork for revolutionary advancements in physics, chemistry, and medicine.

Life of Marie Curie

Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867, Curie’s early life was marked by both intellectual promise and national hardship under Russian control. Denied access to higher education because she was a woman, she and her sister Bronisława made a pact to support each other’s studies. Marie worked as a governess to fund her sister’s medical education in Paris, with the understanding that Bronisława would later help her. In 1891, at the age of 24, Marie finally moved to Paris to study at the Sorbonne, where she lived in a garret and subsisted on meager rations to afford her tuition. She excelled in her studies, earning degrees in physics and mathematics, and it was there that she met Pierre Curie, a brilliant physicist who would become her husband and closest scientific collaborator. Their partnership was a true meeting of minds, united by a shared passion for scientific inquiry.

The Curies’ life together was a blend of profound scientific collaboration and domestic simplicity. Their work was often conducted in a leaky, makeshift laboratory, yet it was there they achieved their greatest discoveries. The couple had two daughters, Irène and Ève, and Marie was a devoted mother, balancing her family life with her demanding research. Tragedy struck in 1906 when Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris. Devastated, Marie was offered his professorship at the Sorbonne, becoming the first woman to teach there. She threw herself into her work, taking over Pierre’s role and continuing their research with renewed intensity. Despite her later years being marred by public scandal and her health declining due to prolonged, unprotected exposure to radiation—the true dangers of which were not yet understood—she remained committed to science. She established the Radium Institute in Paris and, during World War I, championed the use of mobile X-ray units, known as “petites Curies,” to aid battlefield surgeons.

Work of Marie Curie

Marie Curie’s scientific work was defined by a singular focus and groundbreaking methodology. Her doctoral research in the mid-1890s began with an investigation into the mysterious rays recently discovered emanating from uranium by Henri Becquerel. Using an innovative electrometer invented by her husband and his brother, she precisely measured the ability of various substances to ionize air. This systematic approach led to her monumental discovery that the radiation was not a property of the chemical compound but an intrinsic atomic property of the element uranium itself. She proposed the term “radioactivity” to describe this phenomenon. Her investigations then expanded to other elements, leading her to discover that the mineral pitchblende was far more radioactive than its uranium content alone could explain. This single observation suggested the existence of previously unknown, highly radioactive elements.

This hypothesis launched the most intensive phase of her research. With Pierre setting aside his own work to join her, the Curies began the arduous process of chemically processing tons of pitchblende ore in their简陋 laboratory. Through meticulous and repetitive crystallizations and separations, they isolated two new elements. In 1898, they announced the discovery of polonium, named after Marie’s beloved homeland of Poland. Later that same year, they announced the existence of radium, a substance whose radiation was millions of times stronger than that of uranium. However, proving the existence of these elements to the skeptical scientific community required isolating them in their pure, metallic form. It took four more years of backbreaking labor, processing over a ton of ore, to isolate a single decigram of pure radium chloride, a feat for which Marie was awarded her doctorate in 1903.

The recognition for their work was swift. In 1903, Marie, Pierre, and Henri Becquerel were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on radioactivity, making Marie the first woman to receive the honor. Following Pierre’s death, Marie continued her work with unparalleled focus. In 1911, she was awarded an unprecedented second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for her discovery of polonium and radium, and for isolating pure radium. This achievement made her a legend in her own time. Her later work focused on establishing the properties of radium and exploring its applications. She oversaw the creation of a standard for measuring radiation—the Curie—and established the Radium Institute in Paris (now the Curie Institute), a world-leading center for nuclear physics and chemistry that would continue to produce Nobel laureates, including her own daughter, Irène Joliot-Curie.

Impact of her work

The impact of Marie Curie’s work is immeasurable, fundamentally reshaping multiple scientific disciplines. Her discovery of radium and polonium overturned the long-held belief that atoms were indivisible and inert, proving they possessed an inner structure capable of emitting energy. This single revelation gave birth to the modern field of nuclear physics, paving the way for subsequent giants like Ernest Rutherford, who used radiation as a tool to probe the atom and discover the nucleus. Her systematic study and definition of radioactivity provided the essential language and methodology for an entire new branch of chemistry, allowing scientists to understand the transmutation of elements and the complex processes of radioactive decay.

Perhaps her most profound and direct impact on humanity has been in the field of medicine. The penetrating power of radiation was immediately recognized as a potential tool to destroy cancerous tumors, leading to the development of radiation therapy, or radiotherapy, a cornerstone of modern cancer treatment. During World War I, Curie personally championed the use of portable X-ray units, training doctors and bringing this diagnostic technology to the front lines, saving countless lives. Furthermore, the radioactive isotopes discovered through her work became indispensable tools for biological and medical research, used as tracers to map metabolic pathways and diagnose disease. Beyond these tangible legacies, Marie Curie’s life and work continue to inspire generations of scientists, particularly women, serving as a powerful testament to the idea that brilliance, dedication, and courage can overcome seemingly insurmountable obstacles and change the world.
